extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulemaking participants, power plant operators, CCS technology vendors, state regulators, and other stakeholders in coal-fired EGU regulation
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating CCS demonstration for coal EGUs
extracted.subtask_description: Assess whether carbon capture, transport, and sequestration (CCS) technologies are adequately demonstrated and constitute the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for coal-fired steam generating units, including technical feasibility, capture efficiency, operability, and storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated demonstration of CCS components
rubrics_metrics.description: All constituent components of CCS—carbon capture, transportation, and sequestration—have been demonstrated in integrated, simultaneous operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA finds the record shows all components have been demonstrated simultaneously; alternatively, demonstration of the individual components plus a reasonable technical basis that they can function together is sufficient. Examples cited include projects where capture, pipeline transport, and EOR/deep saline storage have all been implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: CO2 capture demonstrated at 90% efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The CO2 capture component of CCS has been adequately demonstrated at a capture efficiency of 90 percent, is technically feasible, and is achievable over long periods (e.g., a year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination is based on demonstrations at existing coal-fired units (e.g., Boundary Dam Unit 3) and corroborated by EPAct05-assisted projects (e.g., Petra Nova). Technology providers and retrofit projects support achieving ≥90% capture across fleet conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability and commercial availability of capture technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Solvent-based (amine) CO2 capture has been the most widely demonstrated at commercial scale for post-combustion capture and is applicable to combustion turbines and steam generating units; other methods (amines, chilled ammonia, solid sorbents, membrane filtration, pressure-swing adsorption, cryogenic) are available depending on flue gas conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's BSER identification is premised in part on amine solvent-based systems; page points to more detailed descriptions in the TSD. Technology choice should be tailored to specific flue gas conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretreatment requirements for SO2 and particulate matter (PM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequate removal of SO2 and PM prior to the CO2 capture system is necessary because amine solvents react with impurities and PM affects capture system performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard SO2 and PM controls should be in place before capture (e.g., wet FGD or dry FGD, electrostatic precipitators or baghouses). Additional quenchers, washes (water/acid), and pretreatment (WESP, demister washes) may be required to limit fouling and amine/byproduct emissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full-stream processing and capture plant availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture plants should process the full flue gas stream (not only slipstreams) and achieve high availability so that the percentage of total plant CO2 captured approaches the capture efficiency metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boundary Dam historically processed only a portion of flue gas for economic/regulatory reasons, leading to total captured CO2 <90% of unit emissions despite >90% capture on treated slipstream. Design/operational choices and incentives affect whether full-stream capture occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrated commercial-scale performance and scalability
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial-scale installations (e.g., Petra Nova, Boundary Dam Unit 3, Plant Barry) that treat flue gas consistent with utility-scale units corroborate that capture equipment, solvents, and balance-of-plant operate at scale and can achieve ~90% capture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project performance (capture rates, tonnes/day treated, long-term operation) is used to corroborate achievability. Projects that treated slipstreams at equivalent MW scales are treated as evidence for scalability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendor experience and guarantees as corroborating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements from CO2 capture technology providers (Shell, MHI, Linde/BASF, Fluor, ION) asserting decades of experience and guarantees that 90%+ capture rates are achievable support the adequacy demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vendors cite long operating hours (many solvents with >50,000 hours), proven processes (CANSOLV®, KM-CDR Process®, OASE® blue, Econamine FG Plus, ICE solvents), and specific capture rate performance (many >90%, some 95–99.8%). Such vendor attestations are considered corroborative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation of known technical issues (fouling, foaming, scaling, biological fouling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical challenges observed (fly ash fouling affecting SO2 systems, demister fouling, heat exchanger fouling, foaming, biological fouling, gasket/material incompatibilities, scaling) must be addressed with identified mitigation measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations include demister wash systems, pre-scrubber curtain sprays, flue gas coolers, booster fan wash systems, upgraded PM controls (switch integrated rectifiers, WESP), additional redundancies and isolations for heat exchangers, antifoam injection optimization, chemical cleaning/shocking, gasket replacement, backup filtering, and compressor component replacement. These are viable engineering fixes and should be incorporated into design and maintenance plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design improvements and redundancy for operational reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Key improvements (e.g., improved PM and SO2 controls, online cleaning, redundancies such as multiple CO2 compressor trains, isolations for in-line cleaning) can and should be implemented during initial design/construction to enhance availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes that many improvements identified at Boundary Dam can be readily applied in new builds and may reduce overall cost relative to earlier projects (example: Shand feasibility study). Redundancy (two compressor trains) enables lower turndown limits and higher availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turndown capability and variable-load operability
rubrics_metrics.description: CO2 capture systems must accommodate variable load, startups, and shutdowns: demonstrated turndown limits for capture plants are ~60–70% throughput historically; a 50% turndown for a single capture train is achievable, and two trains can enable turndown to ~25%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coal-fired EGUs typically turndown to ~40% of design capacity; capture plant turndown should be sufficient to match EGU operations. High duty cycles and average loads of coal units (e.g., 70% average duty cycle in 2021) make these turndown capabilities relevant to long-term achievability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storage and transport demonstration (EOR and deep saline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Storage of captured CO2 through EOR and/or deep saline geological storage has been demonstrated (e.g., Weyburn-Midale, Aquistore), and transport via pipeline to storage/EOR sites is part of the integrated demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recorded metrics such as millions of metric tons captured/stored (e.g., >39 million metric tons transported from Great Plains Synfuels; 550,000 tons stored at Aquistore) and millions per year at Quest/Petra Nova provide evidence. BSER is not premised on EOR specifically, but storage demonstration is necessary to show the full CCS chain works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of federal/assisted projects as corroboration (but not sole basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPAct05-assisted or DOE-funded projects (e.g., Petra Nova, projects funded under OCED FOA) can corroborate demonstration, but EPA does not treat assistance-funded status as essential to adequacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA treats EPAct05-assisted projects as useful corroboration; funding FOA criteria that require technologies be proven and replicable imply basic technology already exists. Ongoing DOE-funded demonstration projects (e.g., Project Tundra) provide additional supportive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy and state regulatory signals as supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws and plans that encourage or require CCS (e.g., Illinois requiring 90% capture for certain coal units, California scoping plans, Michigan and Wyoming clean energy/CCS policies) are evidence that CCS is established and effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adoption of capture-rate-based clean energy definitions or statutory requirements (e.g., 90% capture qualifying as clean) across multiple states strengthens the demonstration that CCS is deployable in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable outage rates and normal industrial variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Planned and unplanned outages at capture facilities are normal; historical outage data (e.g., Petra Nova outages: 41 days in 2017, 34 in 2018, 29 in 2019) and decreasing outage trends inform reliability assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA considers outages unrelated to capture plant operations (auxiliary facilities, extreme weather) as not undermining reliability. Average annual outage percentages of less than ~10% have been observed and are considered acceptable in evaluating long-term achievability.
